title: Tensor closure, cokernels and faithful flat-atlas tests for quasi-coherent modules
statement: Work in the universes of [def-weil-size-convention]. Let $S$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme] and let $\mathcal X$ be an algebraic stack over $S$ [def-sfb-algebraic-moduli-stack]. Use its ringed big fppf site and local-presentation notion of quasi-coherence from [def-sfb-stack-quasi-coherent-algebra], module sheaves from [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category], and tensor products from [def-pur-sheaf-tensor-product]. The structure module and tensor products of quasi-coherent modules are quasi-coherent. The cokernel of a map between quasi-coherent modules, computed in all fppf module sheaves, is quasi-coherent and is also its cokernel in quasi-coherent modules. Let $(a_i:U_i\to\mathcal X)_{i\in I}$ be a small jointly surjective family of flat scheme tests; flat means flat on scheme charts [def-weil-flat-morphism], and joint surjectivity means every field-valued point lifts after a field extension to some $U_i$. Restriction of quasi-coherent modules to $(U_i)_{\mathrm{et}}$ uses the scheme-test identifications of [lem-sfb-stack-quasi-coherent-scheme-restriction] and the small etale sites [def-weil-pbc-etale-site]. The combined restriction functor is faithful and detects isomorphisms. A map of quasi-coherent modules is an epimorphism if and only if each restriction is a surjection of etale module sheaves, meaning that every section lifts after an etale covering. Each individual flat-test restriction preserves epimorphisms. In the big fppf module-sheaf category an epimorphism is equivalently local surjectivity for fppf coverings. No quasi-compactness of the atlas, finiteness of the modules, or exactness of the inclusion on kernels is asserted.

source.place: Tag 06WV, lemma-quasi-coherent-algebraic-stack, parts (2)-(5) and proof (faithful exact atlas restriction); Tag 0GQF, lemma-quasi-coherent-check-exact, statement and proof. Module-sheaf cokernels are sheafified sectionwise cokernels.

proof.text: The structure module has the presentation $0\to\mathcal O_{\mathcal X}\xrightarrow{1}\mathcal O_{\mathcal X}\to0$ on every slice, so is quasi-coherent. We will use the local-presentation definition also in the following form: a module $H$ is quasi-coherent if its restriction to every slice over an object $x\in\mathcal X(T)$ is quasi-coherent. Indeed the covering and free presentation supplied on that slice for its terminal object are exactly the covering and presentation required at $x$ in the original site. All sets and sites below use the stipulated universe convention.

source.place: Tag 06WI (lemma-characterize-quasi-coherent), sufficiency directly from the local-presentation definition

proof.text: For quasi-coherent $F,G$, fix any object $x\in\mathcal X(T)$. By scheme restriction their slice restrictions are $A_T(F_x)$ and $A_T(G_x)$, where $A_T(M)(u:T^\prime\to T)=\Gamma(T^\prime,u^*M)$. Localized restriction commutes with the sheaf tensor product. The big-fppf scheme equivalence identifies their tensor product with $A_T(F_x\otimes G_x)$. The scheme tensor-closure theorem makes $F_x\otimes G_x$ quasi-coherent, hence the slice tensor is quasi-coherent. Apply the local-presentation observation of step 1 at every $x$ to obtain quasi-coherence of $F\otimes G$.

source.place: Tag 06WN (lemma-qc-colimits)(2), proof by scheme slices; descent.tex Tag 06VE(7)

proof.text: Let $\varphi:F\to G$ be a map of quasi-coherent modules and form its ambient module-sheaf cokernel $q:G\to C$. Precomposition to the slice over $x\in\mathcal X(T)$ preserves ambient cokernels by the fibred-fppf inverse-image theorem. The big-fppf scheme comparison therefore identifies $C|_x$ with $A_T(\operatorname{Coker}\varphi_x)$, including the quotient map, since it preserves ambient cokernels. The scheme cokernel theorem makes $\operatorname{Coker}\varphi_x$ quasi-coherent. Step 1 gives quasi-coherence of $C$. Its ambient universal property restricts to the full subcategory of quasi-coherent modules, so this same $q$ is its cokernel there. In particular for every test $x$, the Zariski module $C_x$ is canonically $\operatorname{Coker}\varphi_x$.

For each scheme $T$, use the equivalence $M\mapsto M_{\mathrm{et}}$ from Zariski quasi-coherent modules to small-etale quasi-coherent modules. It is fully faithful, and it is exact into all small-etale module sheaves. It consequently identifies the ambient cokernel of $(\varphi_x)_{\mathrm{et}}$ with $(\operatorname{Coker}\varphi_x)_{\mathrm{et}}=(C_x)_{\mathrm{et}}$: factor $\varphi_x$ through its quasi-coherent image, use the two short exact sequences with its quasi-coherent kernel and cokernel, and apply exactness to those sequences. The kernel is quasi-coherent by the scheme kernel theorem. Thus the small-etale restriction functor on our quasi-coherent modules preserves the cokernels of step 3. Full faithfulness also detects whether a quasi-coherent Zariski map is an isomorphism or an object is zero.

source.place: Tag 06VE (lemma-equivalence-quasi-coherent-limits)(1),(5), on the small etale site only

proof.text: For module sheaves on any of the sites in use, the underlying abelian-sheaf functor preserves cokernels and is faithful. It reflects zero objects, since a module sheaf with zero underlying groups has only zero sections. Hence a module map is epi precisely when its underlying abelian-sheaf map is epi (both mean that the common underlying cokernel is zero), and the general-site abelian-sheaf theorem identifies this with local lifting of every section. This proves the claimed fppf interpretation and the analogous small-etale interpretation. Moreover $\varphi$ is epi in quasi-coherent modules exactly when it is epi in all module sheaves: an ambient epi cancels all maps in the full subcategory; conversely, if $\varphi$ is epi there, its quasi-coherent cokernel map $q$ of step 3 satisfies $q\varphi=0$ and hence $q=0$. The ambient cokernel map is epi, so $1_Cq=0q$ forces $1_C=0$, and $C=0$.

Fix a scheme test $x:T\to\mathcal X$. The representable-diagonal theorem makes $P_i=T\times_{\mathcal X}U_i$ an algebraic space, regarding schemes as spaces. Choose a surjective etale scheme atlas $W_i\to P_i$ for each $i$. The maps $g_i:W_i\to T$ are flat by the hypothesis that each representable $a_i$ is flat on scheme-base-change charts: $W_i\to P_i$ is precisely such an etale chart of its base change to $T$. They are jointly surjective. Indeed a residue-field point $t:\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(t)\to T$ lifts, after a field extension, to some $U_i$ together with an isomorphism of its image with $x(t)$. This is a field-valued point of $P_i$. Pulling the surjective etale atlas back to that field gives a nonempty scheme; a residue field of one of its points gives a further field extension and a point of $W_i$ over $t$. This argument does not require the $g_i$ to be fppf covers or quasi-compact. By the cartesian scheme-test comparisons, $g_i^*\varphi_x\simeq h_i^*\varphi_{a_i}$, where $h_i:W_i\to U_i$ is the other projection, naturally on modules and arrows.

source.place: Tag 0GQF (lemma-quasi-coherent-check-exact), common-refinement paragraph (its V denotes the chosen scheme atlas U); scheme-chart flatness is the representable-flat hypothesis

proof.text: If every small-etale restriction $\varphi_i$ is an isomorphism, step 4 makes each Zariski $\varphi_{a_i}$ an isomorphism. Fix $x:T\to\mathcal X$ and the family $g_i$ of step 6. Each $g_i^*\varphi_x$ is an isomorphism, since it identifies with the pullback $h_i^*\varphi_{a_i}$ of an isomorphism. The scheme flat-cover reflection theorem, applied to the jointly surjective flat family $(g_i)$, gives that $\varphi_x$ is an isomorphism. This holds for every $x$. The formula $F(x)=\Gamma(T,F_x)$ then makes every component of the original sheaf map $\varphi$ bijective. Their inverse maps commute with restrictions by the naturality equation for $\varphi$, so define its module-sheaf inverse. Thus $\varphi$ is an isomorphism. Restriction preserves any inverse, proving both directions.

source.place: Tag 0GQF (lemma-quasi-coherent-check-exact), common flat scheme refinements and reflection of bijectivity

proof.text: The combined restriction is faithful. Given two maps with the same restrictions, subtract them to obtain $\psi:F\to G$ whose restrictions are zero. Its ambient cokernel $q:G\to C$ is quasi-coherent by step 3. Step 4 identifies every restricted $q_i$ with the cokernel of the zero map, hence an isomorphism. Step 7 makes $q$ an isomorphism. Since $q\psi=0$, composing with $q^{-1}$ gives $\psi=0$, so the original two maps agree. This only uses cokernels, without using ambient kernels of quasi-coherent modules.

source.place: Tag 0GQF, faithful restriction consequence assembled from the preceding cokernel and isomorphism tests

proof.text: Finally, by step 5, $\varphi$ is epi in quasi-coherent modules if and only if its ambient cokernel $C$ is zero. If $C=0$, steps 3 and 4 give zero cokernel for the restriction to every scheme test, hence each restriction is an epi and is locally surjective for the etale topology by step 5. This in particular proves preservation of epimorphisms by every individual flat-test restriction. Conversely, if each specified atlas restriction is locally surjective, its cokernel $(C_{a_i})_{\mathrm{et}}$ is zero by steps 4 and 5. Thus the map $0\to C$ restricts to an isomorphism at every $a_i$, and step 7 makes $C=0$. Apply step 5 again. This proves the requested atlas criterion.

source.place: Tag 0GQF, surjectivity test via the common ambient cokernel; Tag 06WV(3),(4)

proof_origin.place: Tags 06WN, 06WV(3)-(5), 0GQF and 06VE(1),(3)-(5),(7); the common-flat-refinement proof, with its isomorphism test applied to cokernels for faithfulness and epimorphisms.
